title: Anthropic ships Claude Sonnet 5.5 at the old Sonnet 5 price
subtitle: The mid-tier update runs about 30% faster and costs up to 30% less per task, while keeping the same $2/$10 per-million-token pricing — Anthropic's answer to the price floor DeepSeek and Zhipu set earlier this month.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic released Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Monday, six days after launching Opus 5.5. The company kept Sonnet 5's list price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, and said the new model runs more than 30% faster and completes typical work at up to 30% lower total cost. Availability is same-day on the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry.

The pitch is efficiency, not new capability. Anthropic is positioning Sonnet 5.5 as the daily driver for well-scoped tasks — bug fixes, document polishing, slides, spreadsheets — that dominate enterprise usage volume. Opus 5.5 stays the model of record for research, hard planning, and long-context work. The split matters because Sonnet-tier usage is where price competition actually lands invoices: DeepSeek V4.1-Flash and Zhipu GLM-5.3 pushed the sub-$1 per million output token floor into the mid-tier earlier this month, and Anthropic couldn't cut list price on Sonnet without repricing every enterprise contract downstream.

This is the third mid-tier model in nine days from a top-three lab, following Opus 5.5 and Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber. All three claim double-digit efficiency gains over their predecessors without a corresponding capability jump — an inflection consistent with post-training improvements running ahead of pre-training ones. If it holds, expect the next quarter of releases to look more like Sonnet 5.5 (faster, cheaper, same class) than like the frontier-capability leaps of earlier this year.

For learners: when a lab keeps the price the same and cuts the cost through efficiency, that is a signal about the market they are in, not just the model. Sonnet 5.5's real story is that Anthropic can't lower Sonnet's price without disrupting enterprise contracts — so they moved the value under the price line instead. Read pricing announcements as competitive filings, not spec sheets.
